subject: blood donor
title: What If Your Blood Could Save 2 Million Babies? One Man's Did

scenes.text: What if your blood could save two million babies? One man's did, and he hated needles.
Australia. At fourteen, James Harrison has a lung removed and survives on nearly two gallons of strangers' blood.
At eighteen, in 1954, he starts giving back. Then doctors find something rare in his plasma: an antibody called anti-D.
Given to a pregnant woman, it stops her immune system from attacking her unborn baby when their blood types clash.
So he donates every two weeks, for more than sixty years. 1,173 donations, until Australian law retires him at 81.
His plasma is credited with protecting about 2.4 million babies. One of the mothers treated was his own daughter. He died in 2025, aged 88.

description:
What if your blood could save two million babies? James Harrison's did.
The Australian donor's plasma contained a rare antibody, anti-D, used to make a medicine that prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, in which a mother's immune system attacks her unborn baby's blood. After needing transfusions during lung surgery at 14, he donated 1,173 times between 1954 and 2018. Australia's Red Cross blood service says his donations went into about 2.4 million doses of anti-D, and he is credited with helping to save some 2.4 million babies. He died on 17 February 2025, aged 88.

first_comment: Doctors think the transfusions he got at 14 may be why his body made the antibody at all. What would you do with blood like that?
